Soft pneumatic arm · controller tests · make_calibrated_sim seed 0

Test Motion Results

Every controller from scripts/compare_controllers.py, with its gains unchanged (tuned on the scored 7 mm, 0.1 Hz circle), on the three test motions of the course project brief (axial, circular, triangular). Plant: make_calibrated_sim(control_hz=100, seed=0), 0.5 s dead time and 0.6 s pressure lag. 5 s settle at 4.5 psi, then 30 s of tracking, scored like evaluate_controller.

Summary

  • On the RMSE (where the tip is at each instant), the delay-aware SMC and NDOSMC (M2) score best on the brief's motions: 2.1–3.5 mm. Holding the arm still scores 3.0–8.9 mm.
  • On shape (the path, ignoring time), PD and Nikoletta's SMC are better on the fast motions: they draw the right shape, but 0.6–0.9 s late. The delay-aware and paper SMCs are on time but draw the path 25–110 % too large.
  • The delay-aware SMC's overshoot comes from its reference preview. Handing it the exact future reference r(t + T) instead removes most of it: 0.54 mm on the 4.3 mm circle (from 2.35) and 0.30 mm on the triangle (from 1.99), at 112 % and 103 % size. This needs the trajectory to be known in advance.
  • On the slow triangle the delay-aware controllers, the paper SMC and Nikoletta's corrected SMC tie at 2.05–2.08 mm, and Nikoletta's has the best shape of the four.
  • On the lab's recorded real-robot runs (0.1 Hz) the delay-aware controllers are best: 1.1–1.6 mm.

The "no prediction" row is not the reference

It is a hypothetical perfect controller that cannot predict: it reproduces the reference exactly, but through the plant's 0.5 s dead time and 0.6 s lag, as any controller without prediction would. At 0.4 Hz the lag shrinks the motion to 55 % and the two together put it 128° behind, so its error is about 1.4 × the radius (12.4 mm on the 8.9 mm circle). It shows what the actuator alone costs a controller that waits for feedback. Controllers that predict can beat it, so it is not a lower bound.

Why our controllers overshoot and Nikoletta's do not

  • Delay-aware SMC: the reference preview (tested). It aims at r̃ = r + Tṙ + ½T²r̈, a Taylor guess of r(t + T). For a circle at 0.4 Hz that guess is |1 + iωT − (ωT)²/2| = 1.27 times too large (ωT = 1.26). On the triangle it keeps going past each corner by about edge speed × T = 4.2 mm/s × 0.5 s ≈ 2 mm. Replacing it with the exact r(t + T) brings the size to 112 % and 103 %.
  • The remaining 12 % on the circle (hypothesis). M2 underestimates how far the arm moves at 0.4 Hz by about 9 % (4.78 mm measured vs 4.37 mm predicted for a full ±4.5 psi sine on S3), so a controller that inverts M2 asks for slightly too much.
  • Paper SMC (hypothesis, not tested). It has no preview. It feeds back a tip that reflects commands sent 1.1 s earlier, through a model that does not know about that delay, so it keeps pushing after the arm has already responded: a high-gain loop around a delay rings and overshoots.
  • PD and Nikoletta's SMC. Their effective gain is low relative to the delay, so they act like a filter: the path comes out the right shape but smaller and late. They never push hard enough to overshoot, which is also why their RMSE is large on fast motions.

The exact preview needs r(t + T), which the package harness does not pass (it gives r(t) only). It is fair when the trajectory is defined in advance, as the brief's test motions are; for an unknown trajectory, a better predictor of r is needed, for example fitting the reference's frequency and phase from its history.

These runs compare controllers with each other, not with hardware. The model-based controllers saturate 20–59 % of commands. uv run python scripts/benchmark_all_tasks.py, docs/figures/benchmark_all_tasks.json.

Actuator delay check

The controllers use T = 0.50 s and τ = 0.60 s, identified from simulator data (grid search over T, least squares for gain and τ; fit error 0.005 psi). The same fit on the real robot's commanded vs measured pressure (16 segment-runs) gives:

  • T + τ = 0.81–1.44 s, centred near 1.1 s, which agrees with 0.5 + 0.6 s.
  • T alone ranges 0.20–0.75 s and τ 0.19–1.10 s. At 0.1 Hz a dead time and a lag both appear as phase, so this data cannot separate them.
  • Fit error 0.2–0.8 psi (10–20 % of the signal): a dead time plus one lag describes the hardware only approximately. The triangle ramps give the longest lags.

Step tests on the hardware would separate T from τ. This check ran from a scratch script that is not in the repo yet.

Reproduce

  • uv run python scripts/benchmark_slide_tasks.py: brief motions, figures and JSON (about 90 s).
  • uv run python scripts/benchmark_all_tasks.py: recorded real-robot runs (about 4 min).
  • Hold-still row: planar RMS of each reference, computed from the same references.
